summary: A 1976 set of comments from the TENEX implementation of the RCTE Telnet option, which reduces network traffic by deferring transmission of characters that will not cause the receiver to echo. It reports lessons learned in building it.

eli5.summary: Typing letters one by one used to send many tiny messages. This note shares what was learned from an idea to send fewer.

questions: what problems did tenex find with rcte
subtitle: Implementation lessons from building the RCTE Telnet option on TENEX, and three problems the protocol left open.

tldr.problem: The RCTE Telnet option promised less network traffic by batching typed characters and cutting echo traffic, but the TENEX team found real trouble when they coded it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists three problems (spontaneous output, interrupt characters and cleared input buffers) and how TENEX solved each one.
tldr.outcome: It is a one-page set of implementation notes, not a protocol specification, and it is useful as a record of what went wrong in an early RCTE implementation.

today: The metadata lists the status of RFC 718 as Unknown, and no RFC is recorded as replacing it. It comments on the option defined in RFC 726.

sections.title: What the Memo Is
sections.content:
Jon Postel circulated this page from a document describing changes in version 1.34 of the Tenex system. He believed the author was Ray Tomlinson or someone else in the BBN-RCC Tenex group, and Ray agreed the comments should reach the whole network community, not only Tenex users.

The code for the RCTE option of the new TELNET protocol had been completed for TENEX. The memo reports what the team learned. See RFC 726 for the option itself.
sections.eli5: A builder finished a new gadget and wrote down what surprised them, so other builders could learn from it.

sections.title: What RCTE Tries to Save
sections.content:
The RCTE option reduces network traffic in two ways. First, characters that will not wake up the receiving user program are held back until a character that will wake it arrives. Second, echo traffic back to the user TELNET program is minimized.

For the echo saving, the server tells the user TELNET to echo the group of characters up through the next wakeup character. Sending this command as the user program is about to read the first character of that group guarantees the echo follows any response to the preceding group.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing every letter of a word, you wait until the word is done and send it once. The other side also says in advance how much of it to show you.

sections.title: Three Problems Found
sections.content:
Spontaneous output. The way RCTE specified it made a correct implementation extremely difficult. TENEX completely isolated the control of input transmission and echoing from the characters in the output stream. Input and output are synchronized by embedding control information in the output stream, which simplified both the user and server TELNET.

Interrupt characters. RCTE has no explicit mechanism for them, so they have to be handled as wakeup characters, even though they actually bypass the terminal input buffer. TENEX put a marker in the input buffer where the interrupt character was. The marker is never given to the user program and is not counted as an input character, and the SIBE JSYS was changed to report empty only when the buffer total minus the markers is greater than 0.

Cleared input buffer. A cleared buffer may hold wakeup characters and markers, so the user and server could get out of sync, and sending a command for each one is infeasible. Instead the server sends WILL RCTE, meaning clear your input buffer and reset your counters. This is the reverse of a normal DO RCTE, so it cannot be confused with normal use and no new option is needed.
sections.eli5: Three things went wrong: surprise messages, urgent interrupts, and a wiped queue. Each got its own simple fix, like a bookmark in the queue and a special reset signal.
